title: Completeness-critic candidates — governance-instance specificity
suite: SUIT — Sustainable University IT Infrastructure & Technology
method: Reading-based transversal pass over ul-it-policy (SUITPOLICY main/argumentation/companion + SUITSOLUTION technical) source .tex. A 'governance-instance' is a concrete instantiation of governance — a specific committee composition/selection rule, a named governance instrument bound to a specific peer institution, a named role-instance model, a single-accountable-owner role binding, or a named external governance committee used as a model — as opposed to the generic governance bodies/shapes the matrix already covers. The canonical matrix covers: the named UL bodies (ANCHOR-ACADEMIC-BODIES = Faculty/University Council; ANCHOR-GOVERNING-BOARD = Board of Governors incl. the council endorsement path; ANCHOR-EXECUTIVE-LEADERSHIP = Rectorate/Rector), the proposal's own bodies by NAME ONLY (ANCHOR-DIGITAL-POLICY-COMMISSION 'keep'; ANCHOR-ICRADP-CARPN), the generic CIO/CISO/DPO role nouns (ANCHOR-CIO-CISO-ROLE), the generic governance shape/cadence (ANCHOR-GOVERNANCE-SHAPE), and peer-institution ROSTERS at the institution level (ANCHOR-PEER-INSTITUTION-ROSTER, ANCHOR-RESEARCH-PEERS, ANCHOR-ADJUSTMENTS-COMMITTEE). It does NOT capture: (a) the Digital Policy Commission's internal composition/selection rule, (b) named per-institution governance INSTRUMENTS (ETH Administrator Rights Agreement) or ROLE-MODELS (EPFL/ETH Data Stewards), (c) named external governance COMMITTEES used as decision-authority models (Oxford Information and Digital Committee, Michigan IT Council, Harvard FAS IT Governance Committee, Kentucky Senate AI committee), or (d) the single-accountable-owner role bindings for statutory clocks/intakes (central SOC owns NIS2 Art.23 clock; DPO-owned central intake / Art.30 RoPA owner).
note: Candidate rows only — not merged into the canonical matrix. Each row mirrors the matrix entry shape (id, kind, title, surfaceForms, genericDecision, action, localizationVariable, occurrences, occurrenceCount, documents, confidence, rationale).

entries.title: Digital Policy Commission internal composition & selection rule (elected-academic chair, non-voting advisory officers, student representative, council endorsement path)
surfaceForms: Chair: an elected academic --- not a member of the IT operational hierarchy; Composition: a compact body of representatives from the departments and interdisciplinary centres across the university's faculties; Advisory members (non-voting): the CIO, the CISO, the DPO, and a student representative; Decision path: the Commission formulates policy proposals that are submitted to the Faculty Councils and then to the University Council for endorsement before implementation.
Digital Policy Commission chaired by an elected academic, with representatives from departments and interdisciplinary centres, responsibility charters, and a service catalogue.
Digital Policy Commission chaired by an \emph{elected} academic formulates proposals
Govern & GV & Digital Policy Commission with elected academic [chair]
entries.genericDecision: Keep the composition/selection RULE as a generic governance-design construct (elected-academic chair, non-voting CIO/CISO/DPO + student representative, council endorsement before implementation) — it is the proposal's own democratic-governance pattern, not a UL-branded structure. BUT the decision path names the institution-specific deliberative bodies ('Faculty Councils', 'University Council') already parameterized under ANCHOR-ACADEMIC-BODIES; bind those tokens to ACADEMIC_GOVERNING_BODIES so the composition rule resolves through the localised body names. The ANCHOR-DIGITAL-POLICY-COMMISSION matrix entry treats only the Commission NAME ('keep'); it does not capture this internal composition/selection rule or its dependence on the named councils.

The matrix keeps the Commission's NAME but never records the instance-level governance design (elected-academic chair excluded from IT hierarchy, non-voting advisory CIO/CISO/DPO + student rep, and a two-stage Faculty-Council-then-University-Council endorsement path). entries.title: Named per-institution governance instrument used as model: ETH Zurich 'Administrator Rights Agreement'
surfaceForms: Key innovation --- the Administrator Rights Agreement: Unlike a total ban, ETH Zurich has formalised root access through an \emph{Agreement Regarding Administrator Rights}~\cite{eth-admin-agreement}
The model draws on ETH Zurich where an \emph{administrator rights agreement} ...
At ETH Zurich, the Administrator Rights Agreement~\cite{eth-admin-agreement} is a legally binding \emph{transfer} of responsibility, not an abdication.
entries.genericDecision: Generalize to 'a binding administrator-rights / acceptable-use agreement (on the ETH Zurich model)' or 'the institution's root-access responsibility agreement'. The instrument is a named, jurisdiction-specific governance artefact of a specific peer (ETH Zurich, governed in DE/EN with the German version legally authoritative per the bib note); the suite uses it as the concrete model for its responsibility-charter mechanism. The generic pattern (a contractual, proportionate transfer of root-access responsibility) is what should be retained; the proper-noun instrument and its \cite{eth-admin-agreement} key are peer-specific and follow the same fate as the peer roster. Not the same as the generic 'responsibility charter' / 'enclave charter' tokens the matrix already treats — this is the named external INSTRUMENT the charter model is built on.

entries.rationale: Named per-institution governance instrument. The 'Administrator Rights Agreement' / 'Agreement Regarding Administrator Rights' is a specific ETH Zurich legal instrument (German version authoritative) that the suite adopts as the concrete model for its responsibility-charter/root-access mechanism. The matrix rosters ETH Zurich as a peer institution but never captures this named governance instrument as an instance; when the peer framing is genericized the named instrument should be recast to the role-based 'binding administrator-rights agreement' and its citation key follow the peer-roster disposition.

entries.title: Named per-institution governance role-instance used as model: EPFL / ETH Zurich 'Data Stewards' in laboratories
surfaceForms: Formalize autonomy through enclave charters (ETH Zurich / Oxford model) and Data Stewards in laboratories (EPFL model).

entries.genericDecision: Generalize to 'embedded local data-stewardship roles (on the EPFL / ETH Zurich model)' or 'a nominated data-steward per laboratory/unit'. 'Data Stewards' is a named role-instance the suite borrows from two specific peers (EPFL 'in labs'; ETH Zurich Data Stewardship Network / DSN). Retain the generic embedded-steward governance pattern; the peer-bound proper-noun attributions ('(EPFL model)', 'ETH Zurich's Data Stewardship model') follow the peer-roster fate. Distinct from the matrix 'classification owner per cohort' construct (ANCHOR-GOVERNANCE-SHAPE / nominated-classification-owner) — that is the suite's own generic owner; this is the externally-named Data-Steward model the suite cites as precedent.

entries.title: Named external governance committees used as decision-authority models (Oxford Information and Digital Committee, Michigan IT Council, Harvard FAS IT Governance Committee, Kentucky Senate AI committee, California faculty senates)
surfaceForms: Oxford's Information and Digital Committee~\cite{oxford-infosec} reports to Council with genuine decision-making authority over digital strategy; Michigan's IT Council~\cite{umich-it-council} and Harvard~FAS's IT Governance Committee~\cite{harvard-it-governance} operate in a consultative capacity.
The University of Kentucky's Senate has created an AI governance committee with policy-making authority derived from the elected Senate~\cite{uk-senate-ai}.
In California, elected faculty senates hold statutory \emph{primacy} over technology-related academic [matters]
At Michigan, the IT Council coordinates across 19 schools with clear responsibility lines~\cite{umich-it-council}.
entries.genericDecision: Keep as illustrative external precedent (these are real peer governance committees used to show the decision-authority-vs-consultative spectrum), but ensure they are framed as a comparative roster of 'peer institutions' governance committees' rather than as the institution's own structure, and avoid implying the home institution will adopt any one of them. Each named committee + its \cite key is peer-specific and follows the ANCHOR-PEER-INSTITUTION-ROSTER / ANCHOR-RESEARCH-PEERS disposition. The matrix's peer-roster entries record these institutions at the institution level and ANCHOR-GOVERNANCE-SHAPE mentions a generic 'IT Council' agenda item, but no entry captures these specific named governance COMMITTEES and their decision-authority characteristics as instances.

The DPC justification and the federation-accountability argument cite specific peer governance committees (Oxford Information and Digital Committee, Michigan IT Council, Harvard FAS IT Governance Committee, Kentucky Senate AI committee) and their decision-authority-vs-consultative roles. The matrix captures these institutions only at the roster level and a generic 'IT Council adds the grid to its agenda'; it does not record these committees as governance instances, so they are a transversal completeness gap to flag as peer-bound illustrative precedent.

entries.title: Single-accountable-owner role bindings for statutory obligations (central SOC owns the NIS2 Art.23 clock; DPO-owned central intake / Art.30 RoPA owner)
surfaceForms: One locatable clock owner. The central \gls{soc} owns the \gls{nis2} Article~23 reporting clock --- the 24-hour early warning, the 72-hour notification and the one-month final report --- while the zone charters oblige each zone to report inward to the \gls{soc} within a sub-deadline. ... a single, accountable owner.

One accountable owner, mirroring the Article~23 clock. ... a central security-governance owner maintains the supplier-assurance baseline --- the approved-supplier register, the mandatory procurement clauses, and the attestation requirements --- while each zone charter binds local procurement to that baseline.
Central intake (one front door). A data-subject request is received and tracked at a single DPO-owned intake point, so the data subject never has to address individual zones.

the Article~30 Record of Processing Activities, owned by the DPO, maps which zones and systems hold which categories of data ... the per-processing lawful basis is finalised in the DPIA and the Record of Processing Activities (Article~30), owned by the institution's DPO.
entries.genericDecision: Keep — these single-accountable-owner role bindings (central SOC owns the NIS2 Art.23 reporting clock; DPO owns the central data-subject-request intake and the Art.30 Record of Processing Activities; a central security-governance owner holds the supplier-assurance baseline) are generic federated-governance role assignments expressed against EU-wide statutory instruments (NIS2 Art.23, GDPR Art.30/35), not UL-specific. The SOC/DPO/CISO are generic role nouns (ANCHOR-CIO-CISO-ROLE) and the statutory clocks are EU-wide; verify only that SOC/DPO are named consistently with the rest of the suite. The matrix's CIO/CISO/DPO entry treats those role nouns generically but does not capture this instance-level assignment of WHICH statutory obligation each role single-owns within the federated design.

entries.rationale: Single-accountable-owner role bindings. The federation defence repeatedly assigns a single locatable owner to each statutory obligation (SOC = NIS2 Art.23 clock; DPO = central data-subject-request intake + Art.30 RoPA; central security-governance owner = supplier-assurance baseline). These are generic role-to-obligation bindings against EU-wide instruments and are safe to keep, but they are a governance-instance facet the matrix does not enumerate; flagged at low confidence because the saferDefault for non-UL anchors leans keep and no localisation is required.
